claim: TRPV1 is an archetypical temperature-sensitive TRP channel.
source: TRPV1 is an archetypical temperature-sensitive TRP channel (Caterina et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Caterina et al., 1997

claim: Heat strongly activates TRPV1 channel.
source: Heat strongly activates the channel, which could be observed at a broad voltage range using a ramp protocol (Figure 1A, upper panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: For TRPV1, the Q10 value is above 20 over a more than 200 mV voltage range.
source: For TRPV1, the Q10 value is above 20 over a more than 200 mV voltage range (Figure 1A, lower panel) (Benham et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1A and citation to Benham et al., 2003

claim: Having high temperature sensitivity at a wide voltage range allows TRPV1-expressing sensory neurons to detect heat regardless of whether the neurons are in the resting state or excited state.
source: Having high temperature sensitivity at a wide voltage range is crucial for the channel's physiological role as a temperature sensor—it allows TRPV1-expressing sensory neurons to detect heat no matter the neurons are in the resting state or excited state.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the properties of TRPV1

claim: Shaker channel activity exhibits much lower temperature sensitivity than TRPV1.
source: Activity of Shaker potassium channel, in contrast, exhibited much lower temperature sensitivity (Figure 1B, upper panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Shaker channel activates upon depolarization to about −60 mV.
source: As a voltage-gated channel, Shaker activates upon depolarization to about −60 mV (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The threshold voltage for Shaker activation was only slightly shifted by raising temperature.
source: The threshold voltage for activation was only slightly shifted by raising temperature.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The average Q10 value for Shaker remained low, at below 4.
source: The average Q10 value remained low, at below 4 (Figure 1B, lower panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Opening and closing of the ion permeation pore in Shaker and many other Kv channels is obligatorily coupled to movement of the voltage-sensor controlled by the membrane potential.
source: Low temperature sensitivity is anticipated for Shaker and many other Kv channels, because opening and closing of the ion permeation pore in these channels is obligatorily coupled to movement of the voltage-sensor controlled by the membrane potential (Sigworth, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sigworth, 1994

claim: At hyperpolarized voltages, the Shaker channel is locked in the initial closed state (C), in which the voltage-sensor is kept in the down conformation.
source: At hyperpolarized voltages, the channel is locked in the initial closed state (C, Figure 1B), in which the voltage-sensor is kept in the down conformation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Kv channel gating

claim: A strongly voltage-dependent transition in Shaker involves the movement of ∼13 e0 gating charges across the transmembrane electric field.
source: A strongly voltage-dependent transition, involving the movement of ∼13 e0 gating charges across the transmembrane electric field (Schoppa et al., 1992; Zagotta et al., 1994; Aggarwal and MacKinnon, 1996), moves the channel to another closed state, C′, from which it can transition to the open state, O, with little voltage dependence.
evidence: Supported by citations to Schoppa et al., 1992; Zagotta et al., 1994; Aggarwal and MacKinnon, 1996

claim: Thermal energy is insufficient to supply the activation energy for voltage-sensor to overcome transmembrane voltage in Shaker.
source: Since thermal energy is insufficient to supply the activation energy for voltage-sensor to overcome transmembrane voltage, opening of the channel is dictated by the membrane potential.
evidence: Based on inference from the energetics of voltage-sensor movement

claim: The high fidelity of Shaker and other voltage-gated channels in reporting changes in membrane potential at variable environmental conditions is the basis for reliable electrical signaling of the nervous system.
source: The high fidelity of Shaker and other voltage-gated channels in reporting changes in membrane potential at variable environmental conditions is the basis for reliable electrical signaling of the nervous system.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of nervous system function

claim: Shaker channel Q10 increased modestly around −80 to −60 mV, approaching 10 at its peak.
source: A closer inspection of the Shaker channel Q10 measurement, however, revealed that it did increase modestly around −80 to −60 mV (arrow in Figure 1B, lower panel), approaching 10 at its peak.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The voltage range of −80 to −60 mV is where the voltage-sensor starts to move in Shaker, permitting the C→C′ transition.
source: It is intriguing that this is the voltage range at which the voltage-sensor starts to move, permitting the C→C′ transition. This can be seen in the voltage dependence of gating charge movement (Q-V curve, Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The voltage-dependent transition in TRPV1 is highly temperature-sensitive.
source: Since it has been previously suggested that the voltage-dependent transition in TRPV1 is highly temperature-sensitive (Voets et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Voets et al., 2004

claim: For BK channel, the separation between the G-V curve and the Q-V curve can be conveniently controlled by intracellular Ca2+.
source: To test this possibility, we conducted similar measurements with the voltage-gated Ca2+-modulated BK potassium channel, because for this channel the separation between the G-V curve and the Q-V curve can be conveniently controlled by intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of BK channel properties

claim: BK channel in the presence of intracellular Ca2+ exhibited a transient Q10 increase at the voltage range where voltage-sensor started to be activated by depolarization, around −80 mV.
source: We observed that, like Shaker, BK in the presence of intracellular Ca2+ also exhibited a transient Q10 increase at the voltage range where voltage-sensor started to be activated by depolarization, around −80 mV (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Removing Ca2+ shifts the voltage range for BK channel activation, substantially increasing the separation between G-V and Q-V curves.
source: Removing Ca2+ shifts the voltage range for channel activation, substantially increasing the separation between G-V and Q-V curves (Horrigan and Aldrich, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Horrigan and Aldrich, 1999

claim: The change in BK channel activation upon Ca2+ removal is achieved mainly through a dual-allosteric coupling between the C′→O transition and the Ca2+ and voltage induced transitions.
source: The change is achieved mainly through a dual-allosteric coupling between the C′→O transition and the Ca2+ and voltage induced transitions (Horrigan and Aldrich, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Horrigan and Aldrich, 1999

claim: In the absence of Ca2+, the transient Q10 increase in BK channel was substantially shifted to around +100 mV.
source: We observed two interesting effects of Ca2+ removal on the transient Q10 increase. First, it substantially shifted the voltage range at which the transient Q10 increase occurred, to around +100 mV (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: In the absence of Ca2+, the extent of the Q10 increase in BK channel was enhanced dramatically even though the total gating charge movement remained unchanged.
source: More importantly, in the absence of Ca2+ the extent of the Q10 increase was enhanced dramatically even though the total gating charge movement remained unchanged (Horrigan and Aldrich, 1999; Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 2B and citation to Horrigan and Aldrich, 1999

claim: The Q10 increase in BK channel may be associated with the activation gate opening (C′→O transition) rather than the voltage-sensor movement (C→C′ transition).
source: These observations suggest that the Q10 increase may not be associated with the voltage-sensor movement (as reflected by the Q-V curve) but rather associated with the activation gate opening (as reflected by the G-V curve), that is, instead of the C→C′ transition, it seemed to be the C′→O transition that yielded the Q10 increase.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations

claim: Both Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 exhibited a surprisingly prominent Q10 transient increase that peaked in the 20-to-30 range.
source: We found that both Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 exhibited a surprisingly prominent Q10 transient increase that peaked in the 20-to-30 range (Figure 3)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: The Q10 values of Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 are at a level comparable to that of TRPV1.
source: We found that both Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 exhibited a surprisingly prominent Q10 transient increase that peaked in the 20-to-30 range (Figure 3), a level comparable to that of TRPV1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: Highly temperature-sensitive activation could be observed in Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 when either a voltage ramp or a voltage step was applied.
source: Highly temperature-sensitive activation could be observed when either a voltage ramp or a voltage step was applied.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 have similar voltage dependence to Shaker and BK channels.
source: As these channels have similar voltage dependence to Shaker and BK channels (Islas and Sigworth, 1999; Dougherty et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citations to Islas and Sigworth, 1999; Dougherty et al., 2008

claim: The substantially higher Q10 values in Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 cannot come from the voltage-sensor movement.
source: As these channels have similar voltage dependence to Shaker and BK channels (Islas and Sigworth, 1999; Dougherty et al., 2008), the substantially higher Q10 values cannot come from the voltage-sensor movement.
evidence: Based on inference from voltage dependence data

claim: The activity of TRPV1 (and other temperature-sensitive TRP channels) is minimally voltage-sensitive (with less than 1 e0 gating charge).
source: This conclusion is reinforced by the fact that the activity of TRPV1 (and other temperature-sensitive TRP channels) is minimally voltage-sensitive (with less than 1 e0 gating charge; Figure 1C) (Voets et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1C and citation to Voets et al., 2004

claim: The energetic effects of heat on the voltage-dependent activation per se are similar for TRPV1 and most Kv channels.
source: Indeed, we observed that the energetic effects of heat on the voltage-dependent activation per se are similar for TRPV1 and most Kv channels (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: The peak Q10 values exhibited no correlation with the temperature-dependent shifts in the half-activation voltage.
source: and the peak Q10 values exhibited no correlation with the temperature-dependent shifts in the half-activation voltage (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 have a prominent closed state inactivation (CSI) process.
source: One noticeable common property of these two channels is a prominent closed state inactivation (CSI) process (Klemic et al., 1998; Amadi et al., 2007; Figure 5)
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5 and citations to Klemic et al., 1998; Amadi et al., 2007

claim: During CSI, the voltage-sensor is decoupled from the activation gate.
source: One noticeable common property of these two channels is a prominent closed state inactivation (CSI) process (Klemic et al., 1998; Amadi et al., 2007; Figure 5), during which the voltage-sensor is decoupled from the activation gate (Klemic et al., 1998; Barghaan and Bahring, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klemic et al., 1998; Barghaan and Bahring, 2009

claim: CSI relaxes the obligatory gating by voltage, increasing the probability of transitioning from C into C′ at mild depolarization.
source: This 'slippage' in coupling relaxes the obligatory gating by voltage, increasing the probability of transitioning from C into C′ at mild depolarization (Shin et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shin et al., 2004

claim: CSI simultaneously makes Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 more TRPV1-like in both voltage- and heat-dependent activation.
source: In other words, CSI simultaneously makes Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 more TRPV1-like in both voltage- and heat-dependent activation.
evidence: Based on inference from the effects of CSI

claim: The Q10 increase in Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 peaked at roughly −70 to −50 mV, where the probability of the channels being not open but in the CSI state was high.
source: The Q10 increase peaked at roughly −70 to −50 mV, where the probability of the channels being not open but in the CSI state was high (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,C

claim: Under conditions where Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 are in the CSI state, both channels could be strongly heat-activated.
source: Under such condition, both channels could be strongly heat-activated (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: The Shaker channel does not undergo CSI.
source: In contrast to Kv2.1 and Kv4.3, the less temperature-sensitive Shaker channel does not undergo CSI (Aldrich, 2001; Zhou et al., 2001; Fineberg et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Aldrich, 2001; Zhou et al., 2001; Fineberg et al., 2012

claim: In Shaker, the voltage-sensor is always obligatorily coupled to the activation gate, preventing the gate being activated by heat.
source: so that its voltage-sensor is always obligatorily coupled to the activation gate, preventing the gate being activated by heat.
evidence: Based on inference from the absence of CSI in Shaker

claim: The ILT mutant of Shaker generates a prominent separation between the Q-V curve and the G-V curve.
source: Two well-characterized Shaker mutants are known to exhibit this property, ILT (Smith-Maxwell et al., 1998) and V2 (Schoppa and Sigworth, 1998). The mutations in ILT generate a prominent separation between the Q-V curve and the G-V curve (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 6A and citation to Smith-Maxwell et al., 1998

claim: The ILT channel exhibited a large Q10 transient that peaked above 20, making activation of this channel much more temperature-sensitive than the wild-type channel.
source: When we examined the ILT channel, we indeed observed a large Q10 transient that peaked above 20, making activation of this channel much more temperature-sensitive than the wild-type channel (Figure 6B–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B–E

claim: The Q10 transient in ILT started near −20 mV where the voltage-sensor has been mostly elevated by depolarization.
source: Importantly, the Q10 transient started near −20 mV where the voltage-sensor has been mostly elevated by depolarization.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The Q10 transient seen in ILT and other Kv channels is not originated from the voltage-sensor movement.
source: Thus, the Q10 transient seen in ILT and other Kv channels is not originated from the voltage-sensor movement.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations

claim: It is the release of voltage-sensor control—through depolarization, CSI, and mutations—that revealed an intrinsically highly temperature-sensitive process in Kv channels that occurs during the C′→O transition.
source: On the contrary, our observations argue strongly that it is the release of voltage-sensor control—through depolarization, CSI, and mutations—that revealed an intrinsically highly temperature-sensitive process in Kv channels that occurs during the C′→O transition.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations

claim: The Shaker V2 mutant has a large separation between Q-V and G-V curves.
source: The Shaker V2 mutant also has a large separation between Q-V and G-V curves (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F

claim: V2 exhibited a noticeable Q10 change at the voltage range for channel opening.
source: Consistent with the conclusions we postulate above, V2 also exhibited a noticeable Q10 change at the voltage range for channel opening.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The V2 channel exhibited a heat-induced deactivation behavior.
source: Interestingly, we observed that instead of heat activation, the channel exhibited a heat-induced deactivation behavior (Figure 6G–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G–J

claim: At voltages where the voltage-sensor has been fully elevated, V2 current decreased substantially upon heating.
source: At voltages where the voltage-sensor has been fully elevated, V2 current decreased substantially upon heating.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: V2 yielded Q10 values less than 1, as seen in the cold-activated TRPM8 channel.
source: This yielded Q10 values less than 1, as seen in the cold-activated TRPM8 channel (McKemy et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to McKemy et al., 2002

claim: V2 and ILT differ by only a few amino acids.
source: It is nonetheless important to note that V2 and ILT differ by only a few amino acids (V2 contains L382V in the S4–S5 linker; ILT contains V369I, I372L, and S376T in the S4 segment).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the mutations

claim: The mutations in V2 and ILT appear to alter gating transition rates and equilibriums without changing the fundamental voltage-dependent activation mechanism.
source: Given that these mutations appear to alter gating transition rates and equilibriums without changing the fundamental voltage-dependent activation mechanism (Schoppa and Sigworth, 1998; Smith-Maxwell et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citations to Schoppa and Sigworth, 1998; Smith-Maxwell et al., 1998

claim: V2 is intrinsically heat-sensitive, which is revealed by decoupling the voltage-sensor from the activation gate.
source: While future investigation is needed to examine this particular speculation and identify the gating transition involved, it is important to note that V2 is also intrinsically heat-sensitive, which is revealed by decoupling the voltage-sensor from the activation gate.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations

claim: Gating of Kv channels can be highly temperature-sensitive.
source: In summary, we found that gating of Kv channels can be highly temperature-sensitive (Figure 7).

claim: A transient increase in temperature sensitivity of Kv channels may have important functional consequences, especially since a change in the Kv channel activity at slightly depolarized membrane potentials would substantially alter action potential frequency and neuronal coding.
source: Potentially this transient increase in temperature sensitivity may have important functional consequences, especially since a change in the Kv channel activity at slightly depolarized membrane potentials would substantially alter action potential frequency and neuronal coding.

claim: Temperature-dependent changes in Kv channel activity profoundly affect neuronal excitability and coding.
source: However, while it has been demonstrated that temperature-dependent changes in Kv channel activity profoundly affect neuronal excitability and coding (Vandenberg et al., 2006; Graham et al., 2008) as well as secretion (MacDonald et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citations to Vandenberg et al., 2006; Graham et al., 2008; MacDonald et al., 2003

claim: How dynamic changes in temperature sensitivity of ion channels affect physiology remains poorly understood.
source: how dynamic changes in temperature sensitivity of ion channels affect physiology remains poorly understood, partially because most studies of ion channel behaviors have been carried out at the room temperature instead of around the body temperature.
evidence: Based on assessment of current state of knowledge

claim: There is a transient increase in temperature sensitivity of Kv channels, which occurs when the voltage-sensor is partially decoupled from the activation gate.
source: A central observation of the present study is that there is a transient increase in temperature sensitivity of Kv channels, which occurs when the voltage-sensor is partially decoupled from the activation gate.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations in the study

claim: The study revealed an intrinsically heat-sensitive gating process in voltage-gated channels.
source: Our study revealed an intrinsically heat-sensitive gating process in these voltage-gated channels.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations in the study

claim: A previous study of Shaker channel activation identified a late transition preceding channel opening that exhibits higher temperature sensitivity than all the other transitions (including the voltage-sensor movements).
source: Interestingly, a previous study of Shaker channel activation indeed identified a late transition preceding channel opening that exhibits higher temperature sensitivity than all the other transitions (including the voltage-sensor movements) (Rodriguez et al., 1998).

claim: There may not be a specialized 'heat sensor' to support the heat activation process.
source: In agreement of Clapham and Miller (2011), these observations indicate that there may not be a specialized 'heat sensor' to support the heat activation process.
evidence: Based on inference from observations and agreement with Clapham and Miller (2011)

claim: An equilibrium process A←→B would be highly temperature-sensitive if the transition is associated with a large enthalpic change.
source: Generally speaking, an equilibrium process A←→B would be highly temperature-sensitive if the transition is associated with a large enthalpic change.
evidence: Based on established thermodynamic principles

claim: For temperature-sensitive TRP channels, a large enthalpic change during channel activation was observed.
source: For temperature-sensitive TRP channels, a large enthalpic change during channel activation was indeed observed (Brauchi et al., 2004; Voets et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brauchi et al., 2004; Voets et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2010

claim: The observation of an associated large entropic change in TRP channels comes from the requirement for the heat-induced transition to occur at physiological temperatures.
source: The observation of an associated large entropic change comes from the requirement for the heat-induced transition to occur at physiological temperatures (Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2010

claim: A simple interpretation of the large enthalpic and entropic changes is that they represent the occurrence of a substantial conformational rearrangement in the channel protein.
source: A simple interpretation of the large enthalpic and entropic changes is that they represent the occurrence of a substantial conformational rearrangement in the channel protein.
evidence: Based on inference from thermodynamic observations

claim: In Kv channels, the conformational rearrangement associated with high temperature sensitivity is not the voltage-sensor movement but rather the process following voltage-sensor movement.
source: We showed in the present study that in Kv channels this conformational rearrangement is not the voltage-sensor movement but rather the process following voltage-sensor movement.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations in the study

claim: Kv channels and TRP channels are known to function as an allosteric protein.
source: Kv channels and TRP channels are known to function as an allosteric protein.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of channel function

claim: For Shaker and many other Kv channels, voltage-sensor movement is very strongly coupled to pore opening.
source: Because for Shaker and many other Kv channels voltage-sensor movement is very strongly coupled to pore opening, activation gating occurs in the sequence C←→C′←→O′.

claim: At hyperpolarized voltages, the strong voltage dependence of the C←→C′ equilibrium ensures that the channel resides in the initial C state, so that the temperature-sensitive transition C′→O′ cannot occur.
source: At hyperpolarized voltages, the strong voltage dependence of the C←→C′ equilibrium ensures that the channel resides in the initial C state, so that the temperature-sensitive transition C′→O′ cannot occur.
evidence: Based on inference from the allosteric gating scheme

claim: Only when the channel moves from C to C′ upon mild depolarization can the C′→O′ transition be observed upon temperature changes.
source: Only when the channel moves from C to C′ upon mild depolarization can the C′→O′ transition be observed upon temperature changes.

claim: CSI in Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 as well as mutations in Shaker ILT and V2 weaken the allosteric coupling between the voltage-sensor and the pore, allowing the temperature-sensitive horizontal transition to occur.
source: CSI in Kv2.1 and Kv4.3 as well as mutations in Shaker ILT and V2 weaken the allosteric coupling between the voltage-sensor and the pore, allowing the temperature-sensitive horizontal transition to occur.

claim: Realizing that Kv channels are intrinsically highly temperature-sensitive has important mechanistic implications for how some TRP channels serve as temperature sensors and nociceptors.
source: Realizing that Kv channels are intrinsically highly temperature-sensitive has important mechanistic implications for how some TRP channels serve as temperature sensors and nociceptors.
evidence: Based on speculation about mechanistic implications

claim: The high temperature sensitivity of TRP channels originates from exceptionally large enthalpic and entropic changes associated with the activation process.

evidence: Supported by citations to Brauchi et al., 2004; Voets et al., 2004; Yang et al., 2010

claim: Large ΔH and ΔS values make free energy change associated with the activation process, ΔG, to be highly temperature-dependent.
source: From the Gibbs equation, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, it is clear that large ΔH and ΔS values make free energy change associated with the activation process, ΔG, to be highly temperature-dependent.

claim: It is generally assumed that the large enthalpic and entropic changes come from a substantial conformational rearrangement in the TRP channels.
source: It is generally assumed that the large enthalpic and entropic changes come from a substantial conformational rearrangement in the TRP channels.

source: The existence of large conformational rearrangements has been directly detected using fluorescent tags in TRPV1 as well as the CLC chloride channels (whose common gating process is also highly temperature-sensitive) (Pusch et al., 1997; Bykova et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2010; Ma et al., 2011).

source: Nonetheless, the structural and mechanistic basis for large conformational rearrangements in temperature-sensitive TRP channels remains unknown.

source: Consequently, it has been highly controversial how these TRP channels sense heat.
